label: Conflicting sources
description: Two reviewed sources directly disagree on the same point — tests whether the model presents the disagreement responsibly instead of picking a side silently or averaging them into a false consensus.
objective: Explain the current evidence on four-day work weeks

plan.title: Four-Day Work Weeks: What the Evidence Actually Shows

sections.heading: What this means for your team

plan.knownLimitations: The two cited studies disagree; this article must present both rather than resolving the conflict on its own.

evidencePackets.excerpt: Our six-month trial across 12 companies found measurable productivity gains and no loss of output when moving to a four-day week.
evidencePackets.conservativeSummary: One trial reported productivity gains with no output loss after switching to a four-day week.
supports: productivity gains reported in this trial
doesNotEstablish: 12 companies, 6 months — small and short relative to the claim's scope

evidencePackets.excerpt: Our analysis found that reported productivity gains from four-day-week trials were largely explained by self-selection bias among participating companies, and did not hold up in a matched control comparison.
evidencePackets.conservativeSummary: A separate analysis found the productivity gains from other trials may be explained by selection bias rather than the schedule change itself.
supports: the other study's gains may be confounded by selection bias
doesNotEstablish: a critique of other trials, not a fresh trial of its own
